column12: The 35v/o SCS-9a-(20v/oRBSiC/ZrB2) CFCC is one of a family of ultra-high temperature, multi-use ceramic matrix composites developed in a NASA ARC funded SBIR.  It, like other UHTC materials, is intended to be used in TPS applications.  It was specifically developed as a ultra high temperature structural material to facilitate attaching other UHTC materials in TPS.  Because of its large strain-to- failure, low modulus, and failure characteristics it may be suitable for many other applications including large panel TPS.  Orthotropic mechanical properties for a unidirectional lay-up (nominally 10 plies) were computed with COSTAR.  These computation were optimized so that good agreement was obtained with measured tensile properties. Thermal properties are from measured values except for the specific heat.  The material is fabricated ply by ply and so other composite architecture are possible are, i.e., [0/90]s.  Consolidation is achieved by uni- axial hot pressing.  This material is fabricated exclusively by Advanced Ceramics Research of Tucson, Arizona.  Because of the planarity and large volume fraction of SiC fibers in this material a oxidation protection coating is recommended for TPS applications.  Such a coating has been optimized for this material by Ultramet of Pacoima, CA in a separate NASA ARC funded SBIR program The coating, called Ultra-2000, is a CVD codeposited HfC/SiC with a nominal thickness of 5 mils.  Maximum single use temperature is based on observed performance of the oxidation protection coating (ULTRA-2000). Parallel, longitudinal or axial properties are in the fiber direction and normal properties are perpendicular or transverse to the fiber. Thin plates of this material can be considered transversely isotropic.

column12: This material was developed as part of an effort to develop low color, ultraviolet radiation and atomic oxygen resistant polyimides.   This was done by combining attributes from colorless, UV resistant polyimides and atomic oxygen resistant polymers into a single material.  It is potentially useful in several spacecraft applications, such as thin film membranes on antennas, second-surface mirrors, thermal/optical coatings and multi-layer thermal insulation (MLI) blankets.  Bis(3-aminophenyl)-3,5-di(trifluoromethyl)phenylphosphine oxide (TFMDA) was synthesized and used to prepare polyimides in order to promote colorlessness.  This material was prepared by reacting stiochiometric quantities of TFMDA with 4,4'-Biphenoxy Dianhydride (BPODA) in N,N-simethylacetamide (DMAc) under a nitrogen atmosphere. The inherent viscosity of BPODA/TFMDA is 0.57 dL/g.  It exhibited temperatures of 5% weight loss of 776.15 K in air and 800.15 K in nitrogen.

It is potentially useful in several spacecraft applications, such as thin film membranes on antennas, second-surface mirrors, thermal/optical coatings and multi-layer thermal insulation (MLI) blankets.  Bis(3-aminophenyl)-3,5-di(trifluoromethyl)phenylphosphine oxide (TFMDA) was synthesized and used to prepare polyimides in order to promote colorlessness.  This material was prepared by reacting stiochiometric quantities of TFMDA with 4,4'-Perfluoroisopropylidienediphenoxy Dianhydride (BDAF) in N,N-simethylacetamide (DMAc) under a nitrogen atmosphere.    The inherent viscosity of BDAF/TFMDA is 0.23 dL/g.  It exhibited temperatures of 5% weight loss of 760.15 K in air and 764.15 K in nitrogen.

column12: Advanced Carbon-Carbon (ACC) is an improved version of RCC, developed in part by LaRC, exhibiting greater strength, increased resistance to oxidation, and reduced fabrication time.  The ACC composites generally consist of PAN (pol acrylonitrile) precursors rather than the rayon used for RCC.  These PAN precursors can be set in a variety of available matrices.  Some of these matrices include modified phenolics, acetylene terminated compound, polyimides and furanic based matrices.  The ACC material is produced by weaving the carbon fibers together to produce a two dimensional structure.  This fabric is then impregnated with resin and heated.  After this fiber/matric system is formed, it is coated with and oxidation protection material which is most often SiC.

Acusil I is a moderate-density, filled silicone syntactic foam in a Flex-Core¨ phenolic-fiberglass honeycomb. The material has excellent ablation and insulation performance and is recommended for use at heating rates up to 2300 kW/m2 (200 BTU/ft2-s).

Acusil I is the thermal protection material on the forward heatshield of the METEOR recovery capsule for space microgravity experiments. Acusil I also has application for the forebody thermal protection system for planetary entry probes.

Arc plasma tests have demonstrated that Acusil I exhibits no surface recession for convective heat fluxes up to 1400 kW/m2 (120 BTU/ft2-s). The Apollo-proven honeycomb approach ensures bond integrity and provides structural reinforcement that allows applications in high shear and/or pressure gradient environments.

column12: AFRSI is a quilted blanket TPS consisting of a woven silica outer fabric, a woven glass inner fabric, and fibrous silica batting sewn together with silica thread. AFRSI is a quilted blanket TPS consisting of a woven silica outer fabric, a woven glass inner fabric, and fibrous silica batting sewn together with silica thread.This construction, also referred to as Type II AFRSI or Shuttle AFRSI, was developed from Type I AFRSI which has a thinner outer fabric.  Type II AFRSI is currently used on a large percentage of the leeside surfaces of the Shuttle Orbiter. A blanket water-proofing agent is typically applied to AFRSI at the factory and again between flights. Currently AFRSI is flown on the shuttle vehicles with a C-9 coating on the outer surface. In addition to meeting emittance requirements, the coating makes the outer surface more rigid and helps to protect the blanket's top surface fibers from aerodynamically-induced abrasion. Compared to tile-type TPS, AFRSI's installed cost is low, but its aerodynamic capabilities are far more limited. It has a much rougher surface finish than most tiles and therefore has an increased propensity to force a laminar boundary layer into turbulence.  This increased roughness can also produce markedly amplified local heating where boundary layers are relatively thin, such as the windward side of most reentry vehicles.  Additionally, AFRSI has less tensile and shear strength compared to tiles, making it less applicable in areas of high aerodynamic loading; especially rapidly fluctuating aerodynamic loads. Although the blanket is very flexible during installation, its surface becomes hardened after application of the C-9 coating and brittle after thermal exposure.

column12:
A development of the basic AFRSI TPS architecture, AFRSI-2500 is a quilted blanket TPS consisting of a woven alumina-borosilicate outer fabric, a woven glass inner fabric, and fibrous alumina batting sewn together with alumina-borosilicate thread. For most applications, a water-proofing agent would typically be applied to AFRSI-2500 at the factory and again between flights. Also, a surface coating of a ceramic material such as C-9 would most likely be required. In addition to meeting emittance requirements, the coating makes the outer surface more rigid and helps to protect the blanket's top surface fibers from aerodynamically-induced abrasion.

Compared to tile-type TPS, AFRSI-2500's installed cost is low, but its aerodynamic capabilities are far more limited. It has a much rougher surface finish than most tiles and therefore has an increased propensity to force a laminar boundary layer into turbulence. This increased roughness can also produce markedly amplified local heating where boundary layers are relatively thin, such as the windward side of most reentry vehicles. Additionally, AFRSI-2500 has lower tensile and shear strength compared to tiles, making it less applicable in areas of high aerodynamic loading; especially rapidly fluctuating aerodynamic loads. Although the blanket is very flexible during installation, its surface becomes hardened after application of the C-9 coating and brittle after thermal exposure. This material has a higher thermal conductivity when measured parallel to the blanket surface than when measured through the blanket. Only data for thermal conductivity normal to the plane of the blanket is given below. Data shown is for a .967" thick, 9.36 lb/ft3 blanket from an EMTL Final Report No. 1817. Conductivity data for AFRSI-2500 of other thicknesses may vary due to its non-uniform density construction. The same report documented some tests on a similar thickness of AFRSI where it had 3-5% lower thermal conductivity at higher pressures and 15-25% lower thermal conductivity at lower pressures than AFRSI-2500.

column12: This material is a low color space environmentally durable polyimide with single walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) used as conductive additives.  Possible applications include use on advanced spacecraft such as large, deployable, ultra light weight Gossamer spacecraft.  LaRC CP2 was prepared by the traditional amide acid route.  The alkoxysilane terminated amide acids (ASTAAs) were prepared by the reaction of 4,4'-hexafluoroisopropylidene diphthalic anhydride (6FDA) with 1,3-bis(3-aminophenoxy)benzene (APB) and end-capped with aminophenyltrimethoxysilane (APTS) at a 2.5% molar offset.  A sonicated suspension of SWNT in DMAc was added to afford solutions with a 0.03, 0.05, and 0.08% by weight concentration of SWNT.

column7: NASA Ames Thermal Protection Materials | Description:
column12:
Carbon fiber reinforced Silicon-Carbide is a ceramic matrix composite comprised of carbon fiber reinforcement in a SiC matrix. The SiC is used because of its excellent oxidation resistance at high temperatures. As it passively oxidizes up to about 3100¡F, it produces a layer of SiO2. This SiO2 slows the diffusion of oxidizing agents to the SiO2/SiC interface, thus inhibiting further oxidation. Beyond about 3100¡F, a passive to active oxidation transition takes place and the products of oxidation change from the solid SiO2 to all gaseous species. The C/SiC material is produced by depositing a SiC matrix on carbon fibers via Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD).

The material was originally developed by Super Temp, and then was picked up and further refined and developed by the French company SEP. Some development of the material and characterization for TPS applications have been pursued by NASA Ames. The material is currently produce domestically by DuPont, and BF Goodrich.

column7: NASA Langley Research Center Database | Description:
column12: This material is made with Amoco T-300/1k fiber/tow.  It was constructed using an 8 harness satin weave (8HSW) fabric, with 35 tows per inch in the warp direction and 35 tows per inch in the fill direction. A hybrid method of densification was implemented which was a combination of the Chemical Vapor Infiltration (CVI) and Low-pressure Pitch Impregnation and Carbonization (LoPIC) techniques. This process made use of phenolic resin, pitch, and CVI deposited pyrolytic carbon. The fiber heat treatment temperature was 2423 K, and the maximum composite fabrication temperature was 1923 K.  The material was inhibited by 20 percent by fabric areal weight, and was coated with PPC.  The layup for this material was 0/90 degrees.

column12: This material is made with Amoco T-300/3k fiber/tow.  It was constructed using an 8 harness satin weave (8HSW) fabric, with 24 tows per inch in the warp direction and 23 tows per inch in the fill direction. A hybrid method of densification was implemented which was a combination of the Chemical Vapor Infiltration (CVI) and Low-pressure Pitch Impregnation and Carbonization (LoPIC) techniques. This process made use of phenolic resin, pitch, and CVI deposited pyrolytic carbon. The fiber heat treatment temperature was 2273 K, and the maximum composite fabrication temperature was 1923K.  The material was conditioned to 2273 K.  The material contained no inhibitors, and was not coated.  The layup for this material was 0/90 degrees, and it was a 7 ply laminate.

column12:
A development of the basic AFRSI TPS architecture, CFBI is a quilted blanket TPS consisting of a woven alumina-borosilicate (or Nicalon NLM 202) outer fabric, a woven glass inner fabric, and fibrous alumina batting sewn together with alumina-borosilicate (or Nicalon) thread.  A grouping of aluminized polyimide film reflective layers with alternating aluminoborosilicate scrim fabric, collectively called multi-layer insulation (MLI), is added to the back (inner) surface of the blanket and attached with quilting stitches. For most applications, a water-proofing agent would typically be applied to CFBI at the factory and again between flights. Also, a surface coating of a ceramic material such as C-9 would most likely be required. In addition to meeting emittance requirements, the coating makes the outer surface more rigid and helps to protect the blanket's top surface fibers from aerodynamically-induced abrasion.  
Compared to tile-type TPS, CFBI's installed cost is low, but its aerodynamic capabilities are far more limited. It has a much rougher surface finish than most tiles and therefore has an increased propensity to force a laminar boundary layer into turbulence.  This increased roughness can also produce markedly amplified local heating where boundary layers are relatively thin, such as the windward side of most reentry vehicles.
Additionally, CFBI has lower tensile and shear strength compared to tiles, making it less applicable in areas of high aerodynamic loading; especially rapidly fluctuating aerodynamic loads. 
Although the blanket is very flexible during installation, its surface becomes hardened after application of the C-9 coating and brittle after thermal exposure.
Data presented here are for a system consisting of an outer layer of Nicalon fabric, followed by alumina mat insulation, and alternating layers of aluminized polyimide film and
aluminoborosilicate scrim fabric.

column12: FRSI is a heat-treated Nomex felt blanket with an OML (outer mold line) layer of white RTV silicone elastomer.   For shuttle orbiter applications, FRSI varies in thickness from 0.16 to 0.40 inch depending on the heat load encountered during re-entry.  FRSI is bonded directly to the orbiter skin using a RTV silicone adhesive.  The white RTV coating is used to waterproof the felt and provide the required thermal and optical properties.  The coating is vented using 0.035Ó holes on six inch centers.  FRSI covers nearly 50 percent of the orbiter's upper surfaces due to its light weight and the relatively low temperatures and heating rates encountered on the leeward (upper) surfaces.

column12:
Graphite/Polyimide refers to any composite with graphite fibers in a polyimide matrix. The graghite fiber reinforced polyimide composites are known for their high modulus and/or strength-to-weight ratios, as well as high resistance to thermal and/or oxidative degradation. These materials are oftrn considered for high temperature applications such as leading edges of supersonic aircraft and jet engine compressor blades.

Processing: The processing information discussed below was performed on composites made with either Thornel 40 or Thornel 50 fibers, TRW's polyimide or Monsanto's Skybond 700 polyimide. The graphite fibers underwent an ozone treatment which resulted in the removal of PVA (polyvinyl alcohol) from the fiber surfaces. A conventional winding technique was used except that the fibers were resistively heated to 350¡ F as they passed through the resin solution resulting in better fiber wetting. After the prepreg tapes were wound, the resin was further advanced by heating. The tapes were laid up in a stainless steel moled (coated with Rulon Spray release agent) and cured.

column8: Hafnium Diboride(HfB2) with 20 volume percent of a Silicon Carbide (SiC) particulate phase. | Description:
column9: There are no current commercial manufactures of the UHTC materials. | Description:
column12:
These UHTC materials were fabricated by uniaxial hot pressing powder mixtures of HfB2 and SiC. After mixing the powders were loaded into graphite dies for hot pressing. The dies were lined with pyrolytic graphite paper that was coated with a boron nitride wash. Hot pressing was conducted in an inert atmosphere at temperatures between 1800¡C and 2200¡C and pressures between 2500 to 4000 psi for 1 to 5 hours. The resulting composites attained greater than 98% of theoretical density with an average grain size of ~10 mm. The material properties are relatively isotropic with no significant orientation dependence induced by the uniaxial hot pressing. Studies have indicated that the SiC improves the oxidation resistance of the composite compared to that of pure HfB2. The UHTC materials are have sufficient electrical conductivity to allow components to be machined by EDM. Currently NASA Ames Research Center has active programs on the processing, characterization and development of these materials for TPS applications, such as sharp leading edges on next generation reusable launch vehicles.

All UHTC material property data are from samples produced by MANLABS, INC. under contract to the air force and published in a series of technical reports (AFML-TR-68-190).

column12: This material is an Imide Oligomer Containing Pendent and Terminal Phenylethynyl Groups which can be used as a high-temperature/high-performance structural resin in applications on advanced high speed aircraft.  It was prepared by reacting 3,3',4,4'-biphenyltetracarboxylic dianhydride (BPDA) with 3,4'-oxydianiline (3,4'-ODA), 1,3-bis(3-aminophenoxy)benzene (APB), 3,5-diamino-4'-phenylethynylbenzophenone (DPEB) and was endcapped with 4-phenylethynylphthalic anhudride (PEPA).  The oligomer was prepared by first dissolving the diamines in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP) at room temperature under nitrogen.  The diamine solution was then cooled via and ice-water bath and the BPDA and PEPA were added in one portion as a slurry in NMP.  The solids concentration was adjusted with additional NMP.  The reactions were allowed to stir for about 24 hours at room temperature under nitrogen.  This solution was used to prepare thin films for the measurement of tensile properties.

column12: This material has a high temperature capability and is useful as a film, coating, adhesive, or composite matrix.  In addition, it is useful as a textile fiber for a variety of uses in the automotive, chemical, and aerospace industries.  It is the reaction product of 3,4'-oxydianiline (3,4'-ODA) and 4,4'-oxydiphthalic anhydride (ODPA).  Melt-extrusion process: LaRCTM-IA powder was melted and forced through an 8-filament spinneret using a single screw extruder operated at 10 rpm.  The capillary diameter was 0.343 mm.  Fibers exiting the capillary were drawn by gravity and cooled by ambient air.  Three different heights were utilized.

column8: Silicon Dioxide, Ludox AS-40, D.I.Water, Silicon Hexaboride | Description:
column12:
Protective Ceramic Coating (PCC) is a dark gray coating for flexible blanket insulations and other nonvitreous ceramic materials. It may be applied to advanced blankets such as AFRSI, AFRSI-2500, CFBI, and other rigid ceramic substrates which require a high emissivity coating for enhanced radiant properties at elevated temperatures. It is composed of H2O, silica powder, colloidal silica solution, and Silicon Hexaboride (as an emittance agent).  It is prepared by ball milling Ludox AS-40, with Cerac S-1061 SiO2, Silicon Hexaboride, and de-ionized water. The coating can be modified with the addition of a solvent and/or binder in order to increase the adhesion characteristics of the system for a specific application. PCC is usually applied to TPS blankets with a 2 to 3 inch bristle brush. The coating has also been sprayed onto fabrics and flexible substrates. The brushing technique tends to provide better coverage of toes and weaves of fibrous material.  The amount of coating that should be applied in order to achieve a specific dry weight per unit area should be applied during a one coat procedure.  Excessive amounts of coating can severely stiffen a given flexible composite and cause undesirable surface cracks in the coating. The most widely used methods of applications are discussed in the current version of the PCC specification.  Applying the coating to blankets which have been previously waterproofed is also addressed.  Please consult with the POC to obtain a copy.
Thermal exposure to temperatures exceeding 1400¡F (760¡C) will rigidize and increase the durability of thecoating.  PCC has survived repeated thermal convective exposure to 2600¡F (1426¡C) on AFRSI-2500 blankets and 3000¡F (1650¡C) on Alumina felts.  The emissivity values shown in the properties section were derived from PCC coated samples of Nextel 440. Note how the listed emissivity values for samples that have been exposed to 1400 K are higher than the values derived from the as-processed samples.

column12: This material was developed as part of an effort to develop low color, ultraviolet radiation and atomic oxygen resistant polyimides.  This was done by combining attributes from colorless, UV resistant polyimides and atomic oxygen resistant polymers into a single material.  It is potentially useful in several spacecraft applications, such as thin film membranes on antennas, second-surface mirrors, thermal/optical coatings and multi-layer thermal insulation (MLI) blankets. Bis(3-aminophenyl)-3,5-di(trifluoromethyl)phenylphosphine oxide (TFMDA) was synthesized and used to prepare polyimides in order to promote colorlessness.  This material was prepared by reacting stiochiometric quantities of TFMDA with perfluoroisopropylidiene dianhydride (6FDA) in N,N-simethylacetamide (DMAc) under a nitrogen atmosphere.  It was also sputter coated with silver/inconel.  The inherent viscosity of 6FDA/TFMDA is 0.73 dL/g.  It exhibited temperatures of 5% weight loss of 773.15 K in air and 783.15 K in nitrogen.

column12:
The fibrous carbon substrate is manufactured by Fiber Materials Inc. (FMI) and is known as FiberForm(R), which is sold commercially for furnace liners. The FiberForm(R) is impregnated with phenolic to a final density of approximately 0.24 g/cc. The ablator PICA shows a particularly high effective heat of ablation at heat fluxes between approximately 300 - 1500 W/sqcm. 
PICA was selected as the forebody heatshield for the Stardust Discovery Class Mission which launched in February 1999.  After collecting samples from the tail of the Wild-2 comet, Stardust will return to earth in 2006 and re-enter at 16 Km/sec; the fastest re-entry into earth's atmosphere, to date, for a man-made vehicle.

column12:
Silicon-Carbide fiber reinforced Silicon-Carbide matrix is a ceramic matrix composite comprised of SiC fiber reinforcement in a SiC matrix. The SiC is used because of its excellent oxidation resistance. Use of SiC fibers gives this material somewhat better oxidation resistance than the carbon fiber reinforced material, C/SiC, but also lower strengths and stiffness at high temperatures. The SiC/SiC material is produced by depositing a SiC matrix on Silicon-Carbide fibers via Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD).

Characterization of this material for TPS applications has been pursued by NASA Ames. Current producers of the material are DuPont and the French Company SEP.

column12:
Aerogels are gels in which the liquid phase has been replaced by gas, leaving a highly porous materials with a submicron framework.
Aerogels are porous materials with the lowest possible weight and conductivity for a solid.  (Minimum: less than 5 X air density, 2% solid material conductivity, 1% solid phase)   Aerogels are typically fragile, but show tremendous potential as low-density, high-temperature insulation. 
Silica aerogels, made of the same components as glass and sand, are also known as "Solid Smoke".
The refractive index of slica aerogels ranges from 1.002 - 1.160 The surface area of silica aerogels ranges from 580-1160 square meters per gram.

column12: This material is a low color space environmentally durable polyimide with single walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) used as conductive additives in order to impart sufficient electrical conductivity into the polymer film.  Possible applications include use on advanced spacecraft such as large, deployable, ultra light weight Gossamer spacecraft.  LaRC CP2 was prepared by the traditional amide acid route as outlined in reference 1.  The alkoxysilane terminated amide acids (ASTAAs) were prepared by the reaction of 4,4'-hexafluoroisopropylidene diphthalic anhydride (6FDA) with 1,3-bis(3-aminophenoxy)benzene (APB) and end-capped with aminophenyltrimethoxysilane (APTS) at a 2.5% molar offset.  The material was coated with a SWNT/DMF (N,N-dimethylformamide) mixture which was prepared by placing 0.0020 g of purified SWNTs in 10.00 g of DMF. a Badger Model 250 airbrush was used to apply the SWNT/DMF mixture to the material.

column7: NASA Ames Thermal Protection Materials | Description:
column12:
Silicone based ablator incorporating a reinforcing honeycomb manufactured by Lockheed Martin and used as the primary heatshield for the Mars Viking Missions. Sla-561V consists of a mixture of silicone, silica microballoons, corks and silica glass fibers. This mixture is then injected into the phenolic honeycomb cells.

SLA-561V was also baselined as the forebody heatshield the Mars/Pathfinder probe which is scheduled to be launched in December 1996 and arriving at the martian surface in July 1997. The main difference between the SLA-561V fore Viking and Mars/Pathfinder is the size of the honeycomb cells and the heat shield thickness. The Mars/Pathfinder uses a smaller honeycomb cells and has a thickness of 0.75 in. The increase in thickness is necessary because the peak heating rate on Mars/Pathfinder is predicted to be around 120 Btu/sqft-s with stagnation pressure of 0.25 atm.

column12:
SIP, or Strain Isolation Pad, is a Nomex felt pad used to prevent stress failure in rigid TPS ceramic tiles. The SIPs are thermal isolators typically supplied in thicknesses of 0.090, 0.115 or 0.160 inch. SIPs are bonded to the tiles, and the SIP and tile assembly is bonded to the shuttle orbiter structure using an RTV adhesive.

SIP can introduce stress concentrations at the needled fiber bundles. This has resulted in localized failure in the tile just above the RTV bond line causing loss of the tile during flight. To solve this problem, the inner surface of the tile is densified to distribute the load more uniformly and increase tile strength at the bondline.

column8: Nextel 440 (or Nicalon NLM 202) woven core, Saffil alumina insulation | Description:
column12:
TABI is a blanket TPS consisting of a fluted core framework that is integrally woven from ceramic fibers (alumino-borosilicate and silicon carbide have each been used).  This core framework has triangular cross-section channels that span the width of the blanket.  These channels are formed by sections of fabric that connect the outer and inner fabrics; all of these are woven simultaneously as an integral unit.  After weaving, the fluted core is stuffed with sections of fibrous alumina batting that has been shaped to completely fill the triangular channels. For most applications, a water-proofing agent would typically be applied to TABI at the factory and again between flights. A surface coating of a ceramic material such as C-9 may be used, but the need for such a coating is not as pronounced for TABI as for quilted-type blankets since TABI has superior durability to vibro-acoustic environments (as high as 170 db). In addition to meeting emittance requirements, the coating makes the outer surface more rigid and helps to protect the blanket's top surface fibers from aerodynamically-induced abrasion. Compared to tile-type TPS, TABI's installed cost is lower, but its aerodynamic capabilities are somewhat more limited. It has a slightly rougher surface finish than most tiles and therefore has an increased propensity to force a laminar boundary layer into turbulence.  This increased roughness can also produce slightly amplified local heating where boundary layers are relatively thin, such as the windward side of most reentry vehicles. Additionally, TABI has lower tensile and shear strength compared to tiles, making it less applicable in areas of high aerodynamic loading; especially rapidly fluctuating aerodynamic loads. 
Property values given here are for a blanket constructed from a
Nicalon NLM 202 SiC fabric.

column12:
These UHTC materials were fabricated by uniaxial hot pressing powder mixtures of ZrB2, C and SiC. After mixing the powders were loaded into graphite dies for hot pressing. The dies were lined with pyrolytic graphite paper that was coated with a boron nitride wash. Hot pressing was conducted in an inert atmosphere at temperatures between 1800¡C and 2200¡C and pressures between 2500 to 4000 psi for 1 to 5 hours. The resulting composites attained greater than 98% of theoretical density with grain sizes in the range of 3-8 mm. The material properties show a slight dependence on orientation due to preferred orientations within the composite microstructure as a result of uniaxial hot pressing. The carbon phase is typically introduced as graphite flakes that become oriented perpendicular to the pressing direction during hot pressing. The UHTC materials are have sufficient electrical conductivity to allow components to be machined by EDM. Currently NASA Ames Research Center has active programs on the processing, characterization and development of the UHTC materials for TPS applications, such as sharp leading edges on next generation reusable launch vehicles.

All UHTC material property data are from samples produced by MANLABS, INC. under contract to the air force and published in a series of technical reports (AFML-TR-68-190).
